summary: Back in Capernaum, Jesus answers His disciples’ argument about greatness by setting a little child among them and warning against causing any little one to stumble.
key_insight: Jesus does not tell the disciples to stop wanting greatness; He redefines it: “If anyone desires to be first, he shall be last of all and servant of all.” Then He takes a child, someone with no standing at all, into His arms.
story: Jesus came to Capernaum. In the house He asked the disciples, “What was it you disputed among yourselves on the road?” But they kept silent, for on the road they had argued about who would be the greatest. {Mk} Jesus knew the thought of their heart. {Lk}

Then the question came into the open: “Who then is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?” {Mt} Jesus sat down, called the Twelve and said to them, “If anyone desires to be first, he shall be last of all and servant of all.” {Mk}

He took a little child, set him in the midst of them and took him in His arms. {Mk} “Assuredly, I say to you, unless you are converted and become as little children, you will by no means enter the kingdom of heaven. Therefore whoever humbles himself as this little child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.” {Mt} Whoever received such a child in His name received Him, and whoever received Him received the One who sent Him. “For he who is least among you all will be great.” {Lk}

John spoke up: “Teacher, we saw someone who does not follow us casting out demons in Your name, and we forbade him because he does not follow us.” {Mk} Jesus said, “Do not forbid him, for he who is not against us is on our side.” {Lk} Even a cup of water given in His name would not lose its reward. {Mk}

Then Jesus warned them: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to sin, it would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck, and he were drowned in the depth of the sea.” {Mt} If a hand, a foot or an eye causes you to sin, get rid of it; better to enter life maimed than to be thrown whole into hell, where the fire is never quenched. “Salt is good,” He said. “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace with one another.” {Mk}

“Take heed that you do not despise one of these little ones,” He said, “for I say to you that in heaven their angels always see the face of My Father who is in heaven.” A man with a hundred sheep leaves the ninety-nine to look for the one that strays, and rejoices over it when he finds it. “Even so it is not the will of your Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish.” {Mt}
differences: In Mark and Luke, Jesus raises the subject, knowing what they had argued about; in Matthew, the disciples come with the question, “Who then is greatest in the kingdom of heaven?”
Only Matthew records “unless you are converted and become as little children,” the angels of the little ones and the straying sheep.
Mark and Luke record John’s report about the man casting out demons; Matthew does not.
Mark alone has the cup of water, the undying worm and the sayings about salt; Luke alone has “he who is least among you all will be great.”

fit.question: Did Jesus raise the question of greatness (Mark and Luke), or did the disciples bring it to Him (Matthew)?

points.label: Silence, then the question
points.text: Mark says Jesus asked what they had argued about, and they kept silent. Once found out, it is natural that they put the question to Him openly: who is greatest? Matthew records that question; Mark and Luke record what drew it out.

points.label: Matthew goes to the teaching
points.text: Matthew often tells events briefly and moves straight to Jesus’ words. His “At that time” ties the question to the same occasion without describing how it arose.

fit.note: One conversation in one house, remembered from two angles; nothing here requires an error.
fit.short: Jesus asked what they had argued about; they fell silent, then asked Him openly. The Gospels record different moments of one conversation.

scene.label: A little child
scene.text: Children had little standing in that world. They had no rights to claim and depended on others for everything. Jesus put the least important person in the room at the center.

scene.label: A millstone
scene.text: Matthew’s word is for a large millstone, the kind turned by a donkey, not a small hand mill. Sinking with one tied to the neck was a picture of certain, hopeless death.

scene.label: Hell
scene.text: The word is Gehenna, the Valley of Hinnom just south of Jerusalem, where kings of Judah had once burned children in sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31). It became a picture of final judgment. Mark echoes Isaiah 66:24: “their worm does not die.”

scene.label: Salt
scene.text: Every grain offering in Israel was seasoned with “the salt of the covenant” (Leviticus 2:13). Salt preserved and gave flavor. Jesus ends a quarrel about rank with a call to be salt and to keep peace.

witnesses.matthew: Builds a full teaching on life together among Jesus’ followers, the fourth of his five great discourses. Matthew alone adds the call to become like children, the angels of the little ones and the shepherd who seeks the straying sheep.
witnesses.mark: Shows Jesus sitting down as a teacher, calling the Twelve and taking the child in His arms. Mark includes John’s report and the hard sayings about hand, foot and eye, so the scene moves from ambition to rivalry to dealing with one’s own sin.
witnesses.luke: Keeps the account short and ends on the reversal: “he who is least among you all will be great.” Luke notes that Jesus perceived “the thought of their heart” before they said a word.

seeing.reveals: Jesus identifies Himself with the least: to receive a child in His name is to receive Him, and to receive Him is to receive the Father. He speaks for a Father who does not want one little one to perish.
seeing.living: The disciples had just heard Jesus speak of betrayal and death, and they argued about rank. Look for the person around you with the least standing and receive that one in Jesus’ name. Deal firmly with your own sin before it trips up someone weaker in faith.
seeing.ponder: Who is the little one near you whom you are tempted to overlook, and what would it look like to receive that person in Jesus’ name?

preaching.big_idea: In Jesus’ kingdom the way up is down, and no little one is overlooked.
preaching.watch_for: “Little ones” ties the passage together (18:6, 10, 14). It begins with an actual child and widens to every humble believer, ending with the Father who does not want one of them to perish.

title: Who Is the Greatest?
